en: Preface:
Among the swift paths to practice, none is equal to the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*nien-fo*). The essential point of reciting the Buddha’s name is that one must first contemplate the mind.

If the mind is not clear, it is merely a waste of effort to move the lips; though the mouth may be intimately engaged with the Buddha’s name, one does not know who it is that is reciting. Now, as for this one...
In accordance with mindfulness, the nine grades are of one accord. Whether upholding the Name through principle or phenomena, none is ever in vain.

If, regarding both the mind that is able to remember and the Buddha who is remembered, one directly forgets them both—such that both mind and Buddha vanish together—then suddenly pure wisdom and wondrous clarity will emerge, vast and penetratingly transparent.
The true realm of quiescent light will be instantly realized before one’s eyes; this is what is called the Amitābha of self-nature, the Pure Land of the Mind-only.

This is the meaning of "earth" (the foundation). An ancient virtuous master said: "Cultivate both Chan and Pure Land; benefit both self and others. When the eyes and feet work together, one reaches the Cool Lake. He further said:

"If one recites the Buddha's name without performing meritorious deeds, entering the Way will be full of hardship and bitterness. If one performs meritorious deeds without reciting the Buddha's name..."

One cannot help but suffer further immersion in the cycle of birth and death. If one performs meritorious deeds while simultaneously reciting the Buddha’s name—like crossing the treacherous fords of delusion by means of a raft—then compassion and wisdom will be harmoniously integrated, and only then can one truly lift up this single phrase, "Buddha. Therefore, you should be diligent and energetic, urgently preparing for your future destiny.
One phrase of Amitābha, spoken with one voice by many mouths; one phrase of Amitābha, regardless of good or evil; one phrase of Amitābha...
Amitābha. The true cause for both ordinary beings and sages. One phrase, Amitābha: liberating enemies and kin. One phrase, Amitābha: universally saving all living beings.
One phrase, Amitābha: ascending together through myriad virtues. One phrase, Amitābha: practicing the six perfections in unison.
One phrase, Amitābha: purifying and clarifying the pure and the defiled. One phrase, Amitābha: uniting the East and the West.
A single phrase of Amitābha encompasses past and present. A single phrase of Amitābha covers heaven and earth. A single phrase of Amitābha realizes entry into the unborn.
With a single phrase, one clearly transcends billions of worlds; throughout the ten directions, the entire body manifests.

It is solely because the friends of the Lotus Society requested instruction on the principle of Chan and Pure Land being but the single mind that I have, without realizing it, let this leak forth. Thus...
This results in a fallacious discourse; though there are words, they have no real connection to the truth. Now, in benefiting others while diminishing oneself, wisdom serves as the precursor.
One opens them with the gate of skillful means and shows them the path of liberation, transcending horizontally and proceeding directly, vowing never to regress.
There will surely come a time when you reach your destination. If you are willing to follow my words, they shall never prove empty.
Written by the Mountain Man of Haikyo Seibai, who has gathered his mind upon the waves, while riding upon the precepts, morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Lying down, I listen to the first crow of the neighbor’s cock; at the fifth watch, the light of dawn gradually becomes clear. Adjusting my robes and tightening my belt, I ponder what matters most:
the ten recitations of Amitābha through faith, vow, and practice.

I only pray that at the moment of death my spirit shall not be disturbed; that I may know in advance the arrival of the time and remain serene in body; that my skin shall shed and the sense-faculties and their objects be purified;
and that I may entrust my substance to a superior lotus on the Golden Terrace.
The great reality of birth and death is truly cause for concern; once the pivotal mechanism is pierced through, ten thousand anxieties cease.
From beginningless kalpas until this very day, when has there ever been so much as a single thread moved?
In the leisure between meditation sessions, I recite the name of Amitābha; To deliver all sentient beings from the river of craving, May those of the nine grades all ascend to the other shore.
Why need one linger with attachment to this Saha world?

Mind after mind arises and ceases like flowers blooming and falling; thought after thought exists and perishes like clouds drifting by. In a single snap of the fingers, one transcends the three periods of time, severing all continuity;
in an instant, the dust of kalpas is utterly extinguished.

One only knows that the Buddha is in the heart and recites his name; one does not believe that the flowers arise from beneath the tongue. The flower is precisely the mind, and the mind is precisely the Buddha.
Where the flower of the mind blooms, the Buddha comes to welcome.
The pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas becomes intimate through contemplation and recollection;
fundamentally, it is of one essence without distinction—provided only that the person recognizes it as true.
Zhaozhou did not delight in it; I alone do. For three days he rinsed his mouth, emitting wondrous fragrance. Within the Dharma-realm treasury is the Land of Peace and Bliss;
where before one’s eyes is not the Western Paradise?
The sun rises in the east and sets in the west; contemplate the vision of the Infinite Light in the west. The great earth, mountains, and rivers are not external objects;
the jewel-like awakening of the emptiness of phenomena is the sovereign of the mind.
In this world, such a human body is difficult to obtain; having obtained it, one must be earnest. How can the boundless and profound debt of gratitude be repaid?
None better than reciting the Buddha’s name to deliver both parents.

Whether in leisure or busyness, motion or stillness, cultivation is not hindered; whether as a farmer, scholar, fisherman, or woodcutter, one may likewise seek it. Whether noble or base, wise or foolish, there is no discrimination;
as long as one recites the six characters, one will find harmony.

The Buddha delivers sentient beings as if they were his only child; sentient beings mindfully recollect the Buddha as if he were their own parents. Without being separated or distant, they constantly remember him;
meeting face-to-face, he remains the very person they knew.
Returning to that realm is truly no going; being born in this land is never not being born. The Great Way leads directly beyond the three realms;
the six streets have never forbidden the passage of people.
In a frantic rush, in a frantic rush—how can this compare to a single phrase of Amitābha? To lay down the butcher’s knife is to become a Buddha;
even seven days of practice is still too much.
Reciting the Buddha's name while at home, one should practice without ceasing day and night, from dawn until morning;
how much more so when at home, where there are many advantages—free from constraints and restrictions, the mind becomes empty.
Abundantly wealthy with a thousand *zhong* of emolument, honored and exalted as a first-grade official—none can escape decline, old age, sickness, and death;
in this fleeting life, strive to reach the peace of the Land of Bliss.
The essence of sentient beings and Buddhas is identical; fundamentally, all are equal and vast. Yet, through negligence, I have again pursued the dust of the mundane world.
Having failed to apply myself with diligent vigor in the past, I have drifted through this Sahā world as a lazy person.
Fools and the deluded do not realize that objects are but mind; day after day they rush about, seeking outwardly. To seek is to know that you cannot find it;
like flowers in the sky or the moon in water, the scene is profound stillness.
Human life is full of affairs and much affliction; even a long life of a hundred years may be difficult to preserve. Amidst the bustle, steal a moment of leisure to recite once:
"Namo Amitābha Buddha"—how excellent!
Whether male or female, all are capable of cultivation; nothing is more intimate than seeking for oneself.
With one voice and one mind, chanting "Buddha," the whole family is sent off to the head of the ferryboat.
This orthodox teaching is heard with reverent resonance; the snowy melodies of the Tuk-ba are skillfully divided. The six-syllable mantra of Amitābha is a truly peerless tune;
its single clear sound arrests the drifting clouds.

When the body is strong and healthy and the spirit is vibrant, one lies ill upon a bed, unable to support oneself. To rouse oneself with fierce resolve, turn back the head, and awaken early is the mark of a truly diligent man of valor.
The oil in the lamp is exhausted and the flame is dim; in blinding darkness, I walk straight into the gloom. When will this long, dark night ever end?
Startled from my dream, I hear the single voice of the Buddha.

Who can constrain one from the three calamities and eight difficulties? Simply by recollecting Amitābha, they shall not exist where one dwells. Delusion constitutes a sentient being; awakening constitutes a Buddha.
It is solely due to this distinction between delusion and awakening that there is difference.
The sun sets behind the western mountains; I long for my native land. One must surely examine oneself and prepare the provisions. Readily pack one's belongings well;
do not wait until the last moment to be flustered by haste.

The burning house offers no peace and lasts not long; how could the conjured city be one's true ancestral home? If you wish to know the Land of Common Abode for both ordinary beings and sages, you must realize that it ultimately returns to the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light.
How many times have I dreamed of reaching the Western Land? There, golden cords crisscross around jade towers and terraces. When the mind opens and the will is liberated, the lotus flowers bloom;
in ultimate reality, how could there ever be coming or going?
I had not yet intended to plant lotuses to cultivate pure causes, when suddenly a verbal message was delivered by a messenger.
Because the worldly path is rife with demonic obstacles, the single phrase "Amitābha" is the body beyond all bodies.
Within the realm of True Suchness, there is no arising or ceasing; within the Dharma of equality, there is neither self nor other. Whether layperson or monk, all have their share:
when spring arrives, where does it not cause flowers to bloom?
The shell of ignorance shattered, the golden cicada sheds its skin; illusions extinguished, the void hangs like the White-Ze Map. In the Pure Land, such monstrosities surely do not exist;
alas, how can you fail to believe, harboring the doubts of a fox?
A single sound of "Buddha" amidst the thickets of worldly splendor; the four-character sutra within the clamor of the marketplace. One cannot leap out from arrogance and pride;
the hoofless iron ox passes through the window lattice.
Flowers of four colors—red, white, blue, and yellow—bloom in full within the pond, as large as chariots. How could ordinary people with mundane eyes ever have seen them?
Only those who arrive shall know that the fruit does not fail to correspond to its cause.
To fully realize the self-nature of Amitābha—what need is there for so much effort? Cease all speculative calculations based on saintly understanding or ordinary sentiment;
with a single stroke, cut through the thicket of entanglements.
When the six sense organs are purified, all Buddhas appear; the sūtra they protect and keep in mind is this alone. One should praise, extol, and believe it;
where else could one find a true companion?
"Cut it and polish it; carve it and grind it. To set one's mind on becoming a Buddha is itself to become a demon.
In this Sahā world, there is an anonymous person who dwells all day long in a secluded, peaceful retreat.
Without distinctions of pure, defiled, or neutral, nor of partiality; in this place, every lotus flower is fresh. This is precisely the time for practice and for making offerings;
why need one laboriously create artificial adornments?
Visualize the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows: What sword is within the treasury of our King? Just look at the single orb of the moon in the sky;
its clear light shines upon you every night.
The first three threes and the final three threes—this dialogue was spoken by Mañjuśrī himself.
An immeasurable and boundless multitude of beings is entirely encompassed within a single phrase.
Those of the lowest grade of birth rely upon ten recitations; though their karma is heavy and their offenses not light, by what cause are they able to join the assembly at the Lotus Pond?
Truly, it is because the power of Amitābha’s vows is vast.

Violating the fast and breaking the precepts is fundamentally difficult to forgive; yet with a single thought turning the light back within, the power of one's vow is perfected. Those born in the Middle Grade of the Lower Level are not few;
the Buddha-moon within the heart is naturally full and round.
Having acted falsely and wrought delusions without shame or remorse, it is only upon being summoned that one realizes the truth of Buddha-recitation.
Suddenly awakening to the fading of sounds and the silence of all thoughts, one stands as a person of the highest grade in the lower level of rebirth.
With deep faith in the sixty-eight causes of Amitābha, practicing benevolence in the world and filial piety toward one's parents,
it is precisely because of encountering a virtuous friend that one attains the lower grade of middle birth and crosses the ford of liberation from suffering.
Those born in the middle grade of the middle level possess the power of diligence; regardless of cold or heat, their resolve remains firm.
Their majestic deportment and minute conduct are free from any transgression, and they are able to produce a single lotus flower at that very spot.
Those of middle grade who are born in the superior level observe the five precepts and concurrently cultivate the ten wholesome paths while aspiring for the Western Land.
Turning their minds toward the Mahāyāna, they transcend the three trainings and directly realize the field of bodhi and liberation.
Those of superior grade attain rebirth upon the lotus; profoundly penetrating cause and effect, their aspirational mind is luminous.
With every thought they approach the secret truth of the Unsurpassed, acting with sovereign mastery within the hundred dharma-gates.
Those of the highest grade who are born through the middle level have minds that do not waver; they are able to cultivate within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Since the original ultimate is itself difficult to grasp, they swiftly return to the source and attain liberation.

For those of the highest grade who attain the highest birth, the flowers bloom spontaneously; they sit majestically and upright upon a purple-gold pedestal. Having perfectly realized the three minds and attained the patience of non-arising, their diligent devotion has not been in vain, for they have come to receive the prediction of enlightenment.
There is no room for debate, much less for thought; to praise it with the lips is already too late. The true Pure Land is the non-arising of a single thought;
few people understand the principle of Mind-Only.
Homage to Amitābha. The Buddha possesses something most extraordinary; it is nothing more than the invocation of an empty name to entice people out of the three realms.
Homage to Amitābha. The Buddha has nothing marvelous; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable—enough, enough, there is no need to speak further.
Namo Amitābha Buddha. The Buddha delivers those with whom he has a karmic affinity. Upon reaching the lotus pond, the flowers bloom without waiting for spring.
Namo Amitābha Buddha. The Buddha-way is inconceivable; suddenly one’s own mind opens, and one enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
Homage to Amitābha. The Buddha possesses great majestic power; he delivers sentient beings of the nine grades, so that they enjoy inexhaustible bliss.
Homage to Amitābha. For the sake of the one great matter, all who are born within my land shall have their heads stroked by me and receive the personal bestowal of prophecy.
"Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—an iron hammer without holes. The void is shattered, and the flowers of the Pure Land bloom.
Reciting the Buddha’s name is not for the sake of meditating on Zen; it requires only that the intent be firm. With a single mind never distracted, one suddenly transcends the three realms.

Reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing Chan meditation are the great causes and conditions for transcending the world. Flowing with the current, one transforms sentient beings; through teaching and guidance, one benefits humans and devas.
Neither reciting the Buddha’s name nor practicing Chan—simply let go of the wild mind and rest. Do not deliberate on good or evil; this alone is the one true reality.
People and self attack one another; for what reason is there such busyness? It has not been bearable for long, and the realm remains unsettled.
The sun and moon jostle toward the heavens; the weary horse at the manger is tethered to a withered post. Though struck, it cannot be shattered—it is but a lump of life and death.
It is difficult to pull back this boat of profit and fame. One knows how many are thus frantic; who would be willing to let half a window of leisurely moonlight go to waste?
If parents are not kin, who then is kin? When both are lost, one sees the person of original nature.

Though I lack the arts to subdue tigers or tame dragons, I still possess this body that wears clothes and eats food. The *nyagrodha* tree has withered and the nectar has vanished; the Deer Park has sung its fill, yet the fragrance of the Way remains fresh.
Since then, I have deeply realized the joy found in idleness; the moon in water and clouds upon mountains are my neighbors.
When it is time to cease, simply cease; what is this body but a bubble upon the water? When enemies and kin gather, emotions are hard to resist;

when loved ones part, do not linger in calculation. As the lotus-drip of the hourglass exhausts the dreams of past and present, and the incense smoke vanishes with its long and short sorrows, it is better to see the three realms as they truly are within the three realms, rather than vainly giving rise to so many idle thoughts.
The act of giving and receiving is like a game of chess; how much better it would be not to become attached at all. Even if one holds the winning strategy alone, one cannot escape destiny;

when the pieces are exhausted upon the empty board, the loss becomes even greater. Do not let floating splendor exceed reality; through the doubts and slanders of others, you remain free from self-deception.
On the ancient roads of Chang’an, travelers are few; often, at the end of their journey, they weep at the crossroads.
Chapter on Filial Reflection:
Every household has two Buddhas. Why is it that people of the world do not recognize them? The parents sitting together in the hall above are none other than Śākyamuni and Maitreya.
There is no need to light candles or burn incense; one simply needs to be reverent and fulfill one's duties, offering simple food and water at all times.

To serve with joy: with a graceful countenance and reverent compliance, one’s demeanor toward their parents’ expressions must never falter; morning and evening, one must attend to their needs and offer salutations without fail.
One should wait upon them for their rising and resting, respectfully mindful of the toil and labor of their upbringing. Their kindness is as deep as the vast heavens and knows no limit.

Now that I have grown to adulthood, I ought to exhaust my heart and strength in serving them while they live and burying them according to ritual when they pass. In the spring and autumn sacrifices, I shall never err; I shall tread the path of goodness through filial piety alone.
This is the foremost. It is the supreme merit in the world. In governing a state, regulating a family, and cultivating the self, there is no principle that surpasses this one.

Observe the filial crow that returns to feed its parents; how can humans fail to emulate them? If you do not contemplate filial piety toward your father and mother, consider from where this body was obtained.
It was fortunately brought forth by the life-giving work of your parents, and all your achievements are established through them. Whether remaining at home or leaving it for the monastic life—
Generally, all beings receive the kindness and virtue of their parents, yet they fail to understand how to show filial piety and reverence to their elders. Even as monks, they provide no benefit.

Our Buddha, the Great Sage of Compassion, even tore flesh from his own body and bone from his own frame to save his kin; one must recognize this kindness and know how to repay it. Ultimate filiality lies in manifesting and clarifying one's inner virtue.
The principles of the Three Teachings are fundamentally the same; by nature, they serve as a model for the world. Throughout one’s life, one should remain ever mindful of illness.
This is a cause for sorrow. When entering or leaving, one must be reverent and cautious; when dressing for cold or heat, one must offer appropriate clothing;

and when providing seasonal delicacies and food and drink, one must certainly keep this in mind at all times, never failing for even a single moment. Reflecting upon it now, one harbors regret for the rest of one's life;
as a child, one ought to cherish every day.
I left home to become a monk in my youth. My father passed away early, leaving only my compassionate mother in her home; my elder brother remained until she reached the end of her natural life.

Our family had long been engaged in agriculture, and by the grace of providing simple sustenance, we were never in want. While I was traveling abroad on pilgrimage, I had no leisure to return for a visit.
When I finally reached maturity and desired to repay my private debt of gratitude, alas, I saw only her passing. Oh, how painful! I reverently reflect upon the care with which she nurtured me.
My labors have been in vain; the debt of boundless gratitude is deep, firm, lofty, and vast.

Having failed to provide them with sweet delicacies while they lived, and being unable to perform the ancestral sacrifices after their passing, I am truly a great sinner in this world. Whenever such thoughts arise, I cannot overcome my grief and sobbing, and tears flow freely.
Alas! Those who gave me life are my parents; those who brought me to completion are my teachers and friends. As I approach the age of sixty—the "near-earshot" year—only...
This longing for my ancestors could not be stilled, so I composed the "Essay on Filial Reflection" to admonish myself:

Studying the Way is like ascending a mountain ten thousand fathoms high; At the summit of the solitary peak, all climbing and grasping cease. One must walk directly to the place where there is no walking;
Only then does one realize that heaven and earth are no longer the human realm.
Above, there has never been a single thing; enlightenment is not a tree, nor is the mirror a stand.
By practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the ignorance of kalpas is reduced to ashes in this very moment.
Before the eyes of one with clear vision, there is darkness for three feet; behind the crown of the Vajra-head, there is light for a fathom.
Performing a somersault upon the back of empty space, he knocks down the Stone Gandang of Mount Tai.
When one is fast asleep, there is not even a dream. The azure sky is clear of clouds, and the lunar disc stands solitary. Where is the true master?
He leaps forth as the three-legged donkey of Yangqi.
The dog has Buddha-nature; its tongue does not leave the mouth. With one shout, soul and gallantry fly; mountains and rivers run through empty space.
The dog has no Buddha-nature; it barks at the gate for Zi-hu. Whenever it meets a person, it bites them once. To have no venom is no hero.

It is easy to emerge from within the gate; it is difficult for the body to exit through the gate. When one encounters things before the eyes, the Way is not known; the Mount Jiuyi stands face-to-face.
I have a single phrase that is not convenient to speak to others: when the tongue moves, right and wrong arise; when words are uttered, they are extinguished in silence.
The myriad dharmas return to the One; it is like a silver mountain and an iron wall. Where does that One return? The mind is empty and one passes the imperial examination.
Raising the "Blow-off-Body" sword—direct, decisive, and exhilarating. Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments; there is no separate "sage-understanding."
A single blow of the staff, a single shout—like a thunderclap and a flash of lightning. Words and paths are severed; the tracks of thought are cut off.

Regarding the public cases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the true decree of the Dharma King: if one does not penetrate beyond mere words and phrases, this remains a sickness of the student's mind.
The false cannot conceal the true; the crooked cannot hide the straight. A thieving mind that does not die is a thief within the Buddha-dharma.
Wisdom is not the Way, and the mind is not the Buddha. Free from marks and free from names, water and sky are of one color.
Lift up the head-word. Be decisive and resolute. When the sentiments of sagehood and ordinariness are exhausted, inverted thoughts are extinguished.
Great doubt leads to great awakening; small doubt leads to small awakening; no doubt leads to no awakening. To fail to realize this is to pass it by right before one's own face.
The Collection on Mind-Only (Concluded)
